#4112. Boltgun 2 and Warhammer Survivors devs Auroch Digital say they're laying off 25% of their staff in now-deleted posts

Not long after releasing boomer shooter Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun II and right before Warhammer Survivors launches in November, developers Auroch Digital have unfortunately given a public statement confirming that roughly a quarter of its current staff will be laid off as part of a restructuring. What's strange — to the point that layoffs are, unfortunately, expected — is that the initial social media posts, on both LinkedIn and Twitter, have now been deleted.

In the studio's statement, posted yesterday, Auroch notes their pride in Boltgun II and Starship Troopers: Ultimate Bug War, both released this year, but "despite that creative success, the same market conditions that have challenged so many of our fellow developers have now also affected us." Apologies to the staff affected follow, with a plea "to partners and friends in the industry: if you are hiring, please consider finding a place for our staff in your studio. They have worked on everything from indie shooters to AAA [co-development], and their talent and breadth is second-to-none." The studio also confirms that post-launch development on both Boltgun II and Warhammer Survivors will continue despite the loss of staff.

This is, sadly, not an uncommon thing to report on by any means. There are layoffs every goddamn week, if not several. This is unique, though, in that in the time between the post going up yesterday and my writing of this piece, the public statements have been deleted. There's an archive of the original image posted here, as you won't find it on Auroch's Twitter or LinkedIn anymore. Even with the barrage of layoff news, I can't think of another time that a statement has been outright retracted within a day. Whether this was posted in error, too early, or some other reason I can't know of, hopefully there'll be some clarity soon and, more importantly, opportunities available for the staff affected.

RPS have reached out to Auroch Digital for comment and clarification.

#4111. Poll: Will You Be Using Zelda Notes With Ocarina Of Time?

With the Ocarina of Time Switch 2 remake, Nintendo is once again using its Zelda Notes feature via the Nintendo Switch app for mobile.

While I wasn't able to access and test out the app's features during the review period, I've been dabbling quite a bit since Nintendo pushed it live for launch. And y'know what? It's fine.

Just like Zelda Notes for Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, there's nothing here that I'd deem essential to the core experience, but if you're after some harmless supplemental material, it does the job.

My favourite feature? Gossip Quests. Provided you've activated Zelda Notes within Ocarina of Time's settings, you can link your phone directly to the software to partake in a little game to hunt down specific locations depicted in photos. Doing so will earn you points, which you can eventually spend on new ocarina songs.

To be clear, these ocarina songs won't unlock anything in-game, but you can access a playable ocarina in the app and learn the songs yourself, tapping and holding the on-screen holes to perform a variety of tunes.

It's surprisingly tricky, and in an amusing turn of events, pressing three holes at once also acted as a screenshot tool for my phone, so I had to go ahead and delete that function in my phone settings.

You can also come up with your own, original songs and share them via QR code. I haven't come up with anything I'd deem even remotely enjoyable for anyone else, but it's a cool little feature. [For the authentic Ocarina experience circa 1998, I need The Simpsons theme, stat! - Ed.]

Once unlocked in the game, you can also view enemies from the Hall of Fallen Foes. The app also provides a wealth of stats, including daily records, and you can also consult maps if you're gunning for 100% completion and test your Ocarina of Time knowledge with quizzes.

Again, it's fine. There are features, like the Gossip Quests, that would have been awesome had they been included in the game itself in some way, and we'd recommend at least giving it a go if you're looking to extend your playtime. (Fingers crossed for a Master Quest update!)

#4110. "Mass Effect was my ultimate white whale": Journey composer shares 20 minutes of music created during talks to work on BioWare's recently cancelled RPG

"It's been hard to see dear friends lose their jobs, and this beloved franchise seemingly vanish forever"

The gradual drip of details about and glimpses at what BioWare were looking to cook up with the cancelled Mass Effect 5 continues, this time thanks to a composer who was in talks to come aboard to put together the RPG's soundtrack. Said songsmith, Austin Wintory, has opted to share around 20 minutes of tunes he put together just as an attempt to explore where he might take things if he did end up being hired to score Commander Shepard's next adventure. Naturally, with BioWare's closure, that hasn't come to pass.

The eight tracks in the YouTube video Wintory, whose compositions have graced the likes of Journey and Assassin's Creed Syndicate, has put together range from a main theme, to intense battle tunes, and the sorts of 'ooh, there's something happening' songs that usually accompany key story moments. The opener, dubbed The Legacy of Shepard, blends pensive piano tinkling with bombastic sci-fi swells. The final track's a funkier remixed version of it. I think my favorite might be track seven, Forever Calibrating, just because it's the sort of relaxed and atmospheric backing tune I tend to put on for ambience while working.

"Working on Mass Effect 5 was my career's biggest dream project, my white whale," Wintory wrote in the video's description. "It is my favorite franchise of all time, and for the last couple years I'd been in serious conversations with BioWare and EA to jump in. My suggestion was to treat the original game's masterful Jack Wall/Sam Hulick score as a starting point, and to build on it from there with deeper use of physical, analog synths and a more tightly interwoven use of the orchestra. But a love letter first and foremost (not unlike my approach to the Aliens franchise with Fireteam Elite).

"As part of the ongoing dialogue, I decided last year (2025) to surprise the folks with an elaborate production: nearly 20 minutes of music, fully recorded and produced with synths, vocals and a large orchestra here in LA. I'd not yet learned any narrative details of what they were planning so this was just pure musical exploration. Receiving the news alongside everyone else that EA had decided to not only cancel the project but shutdown BioWare entirely was a deeply felt loss. It's been hard to see dear friends lose their jobs, and this beloved franchise seemingly vanish forever."

The composer closed by thanking BioWare and EA's music department for giving him the chance to put together these experimental Mass Effect tracks.

While this outpouring of info about what BioWare were up to with Mass Effect 5 is likely all we'll ever get of it, given the folks who were working on it have been scattered to the winds, some fans of the series have begun petitioning for Shep's space adventures not to end up rotting in EA's big shed of disused game IP. Though, surprisingly, they appear not to be teaming that call with the assertion that it should ideally be the same devs who were working on the series prior to BioWare's closure that get first dibs on any opportunity to carry on making Mass Effects.

#4109. Mass Effect composer wants to rescore leaked internal ME Universe trailer to "properly represent my musical vision"

Mass Effect trilogy composer Sam Hulick has expressed his intent to rescore the tantalising trailer for BioWare's cancelled Mass Effect Universe for N7 day.

Hulick shared this plan on X, writing: "Alright. My plan is to release the re-scored Mass Effect Universe trailer for N7 Day. A little tight, since I'm a bit busy pitching for a new game, but I'll see what I can do! I don't wanna rush it, and I want it to properly represent my musical vision for MEU."

The Mass Effect Universe trailer, released last week, was intended for EA and BioWare management to indicate what the now cancelled fifth Mass Effect game would be like. As such, the music and assets were not meant to be seen by the public, hence the rescore.

And it turns out that Hulick isn't the only musically-minded person to plan on releasing some Mass Effect Universe music. Prolific composer Austin Wintory - known for his work on Sword of the Sea, Journey, and Hades 2 - posted 20 minutes of music he shared with BioWare staff back in 2025 in the hopes of working on Mass Effect Universe.

Wintory and Hulick join many who decried the closure of BioWare last week, which impacted 50 employees there, and were a part of wider restructuring that affected hundreds of other people elsewhere in EA. This came only a few months after EA's acquisition by Saudi Arabia's Savvy Games Group and Jared Kushner's private equity firm.

#4108. Xbox Announces Two New Methods To Play Games Through The Cloud

"Starting today, we’re rolling out two previews for XBOX Cloud Gaming."

Team Xbox continues to make improvements to playing games through the cloud, and they've just announced two new methods for doing just that - both launching in "preview" form later today.

The first of these is the ability to use your phone as a controller, which will be available across Android and iOS on supported Smart TVs (including certain Amazon, LG, Samsung and other models) in this preview.

To access this, you'll just need to turn on the "Preview Features" in the Xbox app on your supported TV:

To try it, turn on Preview Features under Settings > Account in the latest supported Smart TV experience. When you launch a game without a physical controller connected, you’ll see an option to use your phone for that session.

The second new method is something called "cloud connect", which allows you to connect using Wi-Fi to reduce input latency in Xbox Cloud Gaming titles. The catch here is that it only works with the new Xbox Nano Controller for now, and even then it "won’t work with every cloud gaming experience yet" during the preview phase.

Here's a bit more about it, along with an image:

Players in the U.S. can preview cloud connect with the XBOX Nano Controller starting today. Instead of a Bluetooth connection to your TV, cloud connect uses your Wi-Fi to connect directly to the cloud server running your game. That can help reduce input latency, so gameplay may feel more responsive. Cloud connect is still an early test, so it won’t work with every cloud gaming experience yet. For now, you can try it on supported Smart TVs and the web.

For what it's worth, it's been rumoured by Windows Central that the "cloud connect" feature will become part of all Xbox controllers in the future, but for the time being it remains exclusive to the Nano.

So, there you go! It seems these will remain in a preview state for a decent amount of time as the team aims to "shape the experience", so be sure to provide feedback if you have any improvements in mind.

We'll leave you with a related story about the new Nano controller that released today down below.

#4107. Steam Frame kernel updated with external CD-ROM drive compatibility just one day after a user asked Valve for it

Even with the importance of physical media ownership in the current era of digital product ephemera, it's often unlikely your PC will actually be able to play the CDs, DVDs or Blu-Rays you have around the house. Internal disc drives aren't common amongst desktops or even laptops anymore, so your only recourse is often an external drive.

One Steam Frame user was hoping to connect his own detachable disc drive to watch movies and play Need For Speed Carbon (valid!) using the headset, which can run both VR and 'flat' games without a separate PC, but found that the Frame lacked the drivers to read a disc. In a very earnest community post, user Aiodensghost lamented that this fact "KILLED MY ABILITY TO INSTALL MY ABANDONWARE FROM 2006. You don't sell NFS Carbon anymore (fuck you very much EA) [...] May I PLEASE have the ability to use an optical drive?" So polite!

A Valve employee by the username gaberowe would respond a day later, simply saying "we will look into this thanks for alerting us". Around ten minutes pass, and the 'deckard-linux-no-oopsies' GitHub repository (yes, it's really called that), which is the Linux kernel sources used in SteamOS for the Steam Frame, sees a commit from Rowe that effectively turns on CD-ROM support. More savvy Steam Frame users can hypothetically install the updated kernel themselves, as this commit enabled an existing Linux kernel feature, but it's likely that this support will simply be added in an upcoming software update.

In a news role where I am continually reporting on generative AI and layoffs, it's nice to report on something that boils down to 'software developer does something cool, quickly.' And, hey, Aiodensghost can play Need For Speed Carbon despite EA, which is always a gift.

#4106. PS5 Exclusive Marvel's Wolverine Off to a Soft Start, 2.4 Million Copies Sold to Date

Sony has officially confirmed sales figures for Marvel's Wolverine for the first time, as part of its recent financial update.

According to the report, the PS5 exclusive superhero action adventure has sold 2.4 million units as of 4th November, 2026.

The game launched on 15th September, so this sales figure is its performance after 50 days on the market.

While it may initially sound reasonably strong, it doesn't make for flattering comparisons with other titles.

For example, Marvel's Spider-Man 2 sold 2.5 million copies in its first 24 hours, and reached 5 million in 11 days.

Last year's Ghost of Yotei, meanwhile, reached 3.3 million sales in its first month.

With Marvel's Wolverine reportedly costing around $300 million to produce, it's seemingly still got some way to go before it's a profitable product.

Previous sales estimates from a couple of analytical firms have been proven fairly accurate, then, but it's always good to get proper, confirmed numbers from Sony itself.

While this sales figure means a fairly slow start for a game of this scope and budget, it's worth remembering that Marvel's Wolverine was the USA's top-selling game of September in full game dollar sales. It was also the best launch month for a Sony game since Helldivers 2.

Having said that, its early momentum doesn't appear to have carried through to October; in last month's PS Store charts, the game dropped to 14th in the US and isn't in Europe's top 20 at all.

So, it's been a success in some ways, but there's still some ground to make up. In a sense, Insomniac's Spider-Man series picks up the slack, having sold around 60 million units total, so I doubt Wolverine's somewhat soft sales performance will be too big a concern for the higher-ups.

Mixed news for this title, then, but overall I think it'll be fine — the game will slowly rack up more sales over time, and it's about to have its first holiday season, where there will no doubt be a spike.

#4105. Japanese Charts: Switch 2 Sales Get A Nice Bump Ahead Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

We are back with another look at the Japanese charts, courtesy of Famitsu, and it has been another big week for Nintendo.

On the software side of things, Nintendo Switch Sports Resort continues to lead the charge, holding onto its pole position from last week with another ~23,000 units to its name. The Switch 2 edition of Minecraft also makes its chart debut this time, grabbing a podium spot at third.

Elsewhere, Final Fantasy Resonance continues to perform well on both Switch 2 and PS5, and Hello Kitty Party Land has made its chart debut in seventh and eighth on Switch 2 and 1 respectively.

The Nintendo big hitter this week comes on the hardware end, where Switch 2 has seen a decent bump from the ~mid-20,000s we usually see to a meaty 68,733 sales. We can only assume that this is thanks to the swanky new Zelda Special Edition model and in anticipation of Ocarina of Time, which, when these numbers were recorded, was only a matter of days away.

The PS5 family once again wins the combined SKU race this week, coming in with a total of 16,235, while the Switch 1 followed behind with 5,853 weekly sales.

#4104. Valve addresses Steam's AI game cloning problem - by suggesting developers make their games less copyable

"Rather than relying on a single mechanic that someone can easily copy..."

Valve has responded to the worrying trend of games being cloned using generative-AI and sold on Steam, but instead of admonishing those games or promising to do something about them, it appears to have put the onus on developers to make their games less copyable.

Valve's business team members Tom Giardino and Marc Wilkinson were reportedly asked at a Steam Indie Connect developer conference in Korea, reported by InvenGlobal, whether Steam had any protective measures in place to stop games being cloned by AI. The questioner, a developer, cited an example whereby developers were held to ransom by people threatening to clone a game.

It was in response that example that Giardino - after saying this was the first he'd heard of ransoming, and that probably it was an issue for law enforcement, though Valve would "help in whatever way we can" - outlined not what Valve was doing to clamp down on this, but what developers could do to guard against it. Indeed, Giardino began by underlining Valve's hands-off stance towards AI use, reportedly stating: "We don't want to be gatekeepers telling developers which tools they should or shouldn't use."

Instead, developers can guard against copycats by building active communities and establishing trust and by making a legitimate version of a game the best version available, Giardino reportedly said. Then there's the game itself: a more complex game will be harder to copy. "Rather than relying on a single mechanic that someone can easily copy, you need to keep growing your game by adding features, personality, and creativity that stem from your own perspective," Giardino reportedly said.

It's worth remembering Valve's comments here come second-hand, and via machine translation which InvenGlobal has separately verified with a native Korean speaker; we're asking Valve for clarification. But they also come after the widely publicised case of Needle in a Haystack Simulator, a simple indie game which isn't even out yet, but has been copied so many times it's hard to know which game is the original. The game's developer has resorted to joking that they're implementing a new game mode where you have to find the original game amidst a pile of copycats.

Without Valve's intervention, it's hard to see what a developer can do to guard against this. How can you build a community and trust, and ensure your game is the best version available, if you're not given a chance at finding an audience to begin with?

Plus, the sheer number of copycats makes this a whack-a-mole situation for containment, which is something that - without Valve's help - probably requires expensive legal resources anyway, which in turn is probably out of reach for many indie developers. Also, legal reprimands usually don't occur until long after the damage has been done.

This wouldn't be the first time Valve has distanced itself from moderating what's sold on its PC platform. Indeed in 2018, amidst growing concern about the kinds of games available on Steam, Valve seemed to back away entirely from taking responsibility.

"We've decided that the right approach is to allow everything onto the Steam Store," Valve's Erik Johnson said at the time, "except for things that we decide are illegal, or straight up trolling." It's a stance that former Eurogamer editor Oli called "arrogant and cowardly".

More recently, the pendulum swung the other way when Valve threw an undiscerning net over an entire sector of 'adult' games, catching in it a slew of well-meaning, artistically mature games, as well as those of a more crass nature. And with Steam growing every year, and more games being released on the platform than ever before, the everpresent issue of moderation is certainly not going to disappear.

#4103. Life is Strange makers Don't Nod face layoffs and possible insolvency, French workers union STJV state

Le Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Vidéo, a French game workers union, have released a statement detailing the current status of Don't Nod, the studio behind Life is Strange and Lost Records: Bloom and Rage. The studio's fate has been precarious for some time, but STJV now say that the studio has announced ("to financial press before the employees, as has been its MO") that it is under a "safeguard procedure" to avoid complete insolvency due to an inability to pay off its debts.

The studio's CEO, Oskar Guilbert, told employees that "a safeguarding process is an act of anticipation", in reference to the fact that last year, the CSE (employee representatives) were presented with two outcomes: either future games would find funding and staff would still be laid off, or no funding would be acquired, and the company would be liquidated. It seems the latter is now likely to come to pass, as STJV state that the company does not even have the funds to complete its pre-existing redundancies plan for laid-off employees. The union also note that "the CEO finished his address with empty remarks on how much attention was paid to employees, which everyone knows was bullshit and probably written by ChatGPT."

The statement goes on to clarify that the company will be unable to complete the last remaining project that was in development, referred to as P14. This is due to a huge incoming swathe of layoffs, which include "nearly all of the non-managerial jobs":

"6/6 animators, 3/3 character artists, 3/3 concept artists, 8/10 environmental artists, 2/3 sound designers, 4/8 game designers, 3/5 level designers, 6/6 associate producers, 18/22 programmers, 3/5 QA testers, 2/3 devops, 3/4 HR…

"Management is extremely clearly going for heavily individualized targeting and hasn’t been shy about their intent to keep selected people in rather than jobs, which is illegal."

In an apparent attempt to keep the studio running despite obliterating its staff, "management is betting its all on outsourcing", expecting managers to be able to keep things moving as normal despite the alleged shift to outsourcing and contractors taking on the existing work of fired staff. STJV put it better than I could: "Anyone with a little experience with video games production and sanity understands how out-of-touch such a plan is. The costs of outsourcing a project that was mostly internal up until now and the loss of the experience gained all throughout production seem to have been ignored in favour of short-term penny-pinching with unclear upsides."

The article closes by claiming that the CSE's negotiations with Don't Nod were essentially a farce, as the company had no intent of negotiating in the first place; "Management declares that it cannot offer anything: it’ll be the strict legal minimum and you’ll be glad for it." Concerns regarding the future of the studio have seemingly been made clear by the CSE for years, reportedly living with a sword of Damocles over their heads due to repeated mismanagement, miscommunication and gaslighting, but the future looks bleak. "They ignored the CSE, middle managers, the STJV, financial auditors, all because they believed unyieldingly that a miracle would come and they’d find funds for a game that was too big, too ambitious and ultimately too expensive."

The CSE consultation will reach its end on November 3rd, following which "the regional agency for employment and industry will have 21 days to decide on the plan, and if it is accepted, people could get their firing letters on November 25th." Though, if it is rejected, management would have to figure out a way forward other than insolvency, "because, as you might have gathered, planning for contingencies isn’t their forte."

#4102. Capcom's golden streak continues as Onimusha and Pragmata sell well, but Monster Hunter Wilds conspicuously absent from financial report

Capcom has revealed updated sales figures for its new and successful games, including Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Pragmata, and Resident Evil Requiem. But for some reason, Monster Hunter Wilds is absent from the report.

Capcom's half-year report, for the period running 1st April to 30th September, saw growth in both revenue and profit across nearly all segments of the business. In games, much of that was driven by digital sales, which continue to account for the vast majority of the publisher's income.

The first half of FY2026 was especially strong for Capcom owing to the release of multiple critically acclaimed and financially successful titles. Onimusha: Way of the Sword has now sold over 1.7m copies, up from the 1m it sold at launch. Pragmata, another critical and financial hit, has grown its tally to 2.7m copies, more than double what it sold in its first two days of release. Resident Evil Requiem, meanwhile, has now surpassed 8.5m copies sold.

As part of the same report, Capcom also recorded its highest-ever number of unit sales for the first half of any fiscal year. This is attributed to Capcom's strong back-catalogue of titles, and regular sales and discounts.

But Capcom did not reference Monster Hunter Wilds sales at all in the report. The publisher did not share updated sales for the game, despite sharing a milestone for predecessor Monster Hunter: World, which is now well past 30m copies sold.

Although Wilds was incredibly successful at launch, the game's player base tapered off dramatically shortly afterwards. Capcom offered a sales update in last year's version of the same report, where it was revealed that MH Wilds had sold close to 11m copies overall, but the publisher hasn't offered an update since.

What does this mean - have sales slowed so significantly as to not be worth mentioning? Perhaps. But given that Wilds is coming to Switch 2 this December, and with the Ascendance expansion due for release next year, there's fuel in the tank yet.

#4101. STALKER 2's latest update expands its A-Life NPC simulation bubble, seemingly without a scary performance tax

STALKER 2: Heart of Chornobyl has a new update out, 2.1, which builds on the excellent 2.0 patch by upgrading that most beloved and contentious of STALKER series features: the A-Life system that governs simulated NPC behavior. With the 2.1 update. It's now possible to whack up the distance at which A-Life NPCs (who, unlike scripted characters, will wander around, fight others over faction turf, and sometimes hunker down for a campfire-side guitar sesh) are visualised, while audio tweaks can make these unplanned shootouts audible from further away. The effect, in theory, is a better sense of the Zone's inhabitants going about their bang-banging business, even if Mr. Main Character here isn't close by.

Both the updated game and the accompanying blog post warn that cranking this A-Life bubble up beyond the lowest, default 'Recommended' setting may have adverse effects, ranging from lower framerates to "story quest instability" and crashes. Fearing a return to STALKER 2's bug-ridden early days, I tried out the new A-Life distance options on the RPS test rig, and found they're not actually that perilous – though they might do strange things with binoculars.

To judge the performance effect, I ran the rig's RTX 4060 at 1080p, with Quality-level DLSS and the High preset - save for having the draw distance setting on Epic, to maximise the potential visualisation. Walking through an open, A-Life-ripe patch of the Zone produced a 93fps average on Recommended, which remained unchanged on the Extended setting, before barely dropping to 91fps on the Highly Extended, Maximum and Dynamic settings. Well that's not so bad! The warnings made it sound like the bigger options would ignite the air around my graphics card and brainwarp quest NPCs into thinking they were in Barbie Horse Ride & Rescue (available now on Steam). 2fps? That's nothing. Nothing.

Granted, results may vary depending on your PC specs; the RTX 4060 isn't especially potent but it was backed up by a good CPU and a healthy 32GB of RAM, which likely helped handle the extra computations required for a wider sprawl of distant gunfights. To get a fuller picture, I did try a different approach, leaving ground level to claim a lofty concrete vantage point and- god dammit, recently added fog effects.

Still, the Zone's unknowable RNG calculations were not kind, and after several minutes of fruitless waiting I returned to run more tests on terra firma.

I ultimately didn't find anything else that would suggest an unacceptable risk of performance loss or instability, though I did discover one quirk of the new system: in addition to render distance, your choice of A-Life setting also appears to influence the range at which faction markers show up on binoculars.

More strangely, selecting Maximum A-Life also seems to… increase the zoom of binoculars? As you can see in those two shots, which were snapped from the same position. I guess it's a bug but hey, if GSC are telling me I can get better NPC simulation and a magnification upgrade for the low, low price of two frames per second, I'll take that deal.

STALKER 2 2.1 is out now for everyone. Besides the A-Life distance gubbins, it also adds the ability to tag along with roaming fellow stalkers, turning them into mobile fast travel stations - though, in keeping with the notion that NPCs don't actually give a toss about you, they'll only warp you to places that their specific patrol route was passing anyway.

#4099. PS6 Development on Track, Sony Making 'Solid Progress' Towards Next-Gen

Work on the PS6 and the next console generation as a whole is currently "progressing as scheduled" at PlayStation, it's been confirmed.

Speaking alongside the release of Sony's latest quarterly financial results, CFO Lin Tao said the company is on track to deliver its next PlayStation system, and it intends to make "solid progress" towards the next generation within the next fiscal year (via VGC).

The quote from Tao reads: "Looking ahead to the next fiscal year, we aim to continue to enhance user engagement and further strengthen monetisation through the release of strong titles and the expansion of our service. We also intend to make solid progress in preparing for the next-generation platform."

Tao continued by talking up "investment in the new platform" from the start of the next fiscal year. It has to attach "great importance" to a new console and "make the necessary investments" for it. "We have to support the soundness of our platform and think about how rationally we can invest in that platform. We will announce that at an appropriate time in the future."

A few months ago, Sony CEO Hiroki Totoki claimed the firm hadn't yet decided when the PS6 will come out. Consistent rumours point to a release in the next few years, however, with a potential $1,000+ price point and a handheld device to go with it.

With the prices of components still on the rise — which Sony would need to manufacture PS6 hardware — the potential cost of a next-gen machine looks like it'll be the biggest factor in whether PlayStation fans jump on board or not. When we polled Push Square users, 65% of you said you wouldn't pay four figures for a video game console.

Microsoft will also have a new Xbox to launch in the coming years, currently codenamed Xbox Helix, and that's suggested to cost as much as $1,800, depending on whether it decides to subsidise the box. PS6 is at least rumoured to be cheaper to make than Xbox Helix, so the cost shouldn't get quite that high.

Elsewhere in its financial report, Sony confirmed PS5 sales have reached 97.9 million. With a boost from GTA 6, it should hit the 100 million sales milestone by the end of the next quarter, and become the fourth PlayStation system to do so.

#4098. "Every piece is unified": Dark Messiah of Might and Magic returns with co-op, an Adventure mode, a level generator and New Game+ in the 64-bit Community Edition

First announced back in March, Dark Messiah of Might and Magic: Community Edition is a fan-made mod (for Dark Messiah of Might and Magic, obvs) that spruces up Arkane's 2006 RPG, including upgrading it to a newer version of the Source engine. Details have been scarce since then, but an updated Steam page confirms what other additions the mod – which is being made with the blessing of both Valve and original publishers Ubisoft – is making.

For one, as the Community Edition is rebuilt from the ground up using the contemporary Source SDK, the change in engine allows for both native Linux and Windows 64-bit support. Quality of life features like controller support are also listed, as are achievements, but the shining feature is the addition of co-op multiplayer, which will use Steamworks for P2P connections and hosting. So too will a "renewed" mutliplayer component, based on the original game's PvP mode. The Community Edition also boasts that "Every piece is unified. What you see in Singleplayer is accessible in Multiplayer, and visa-versa!"

Popular Dark Messiah mods that have existed for years have also been folded into the Community Edition, such as a New Game+ mode, a new Adventure Mode structure offering bonus levels and challenges, the addition of sliding as a movement mechanic, new spells, new weapons, new transformations; I mean, it's a mod attempting to gather up twenty years of modding into one rebuilt package, so you can imagine there's a lot here.

The community label extends to ensuring the community itself can contribute as they wish, with modders outside of the team granted tools to create custom elements, maps, and quests, alongside full Steam Workshop integration. While it isn't directly mentioned in the Steam page, the mod's development team wiltOS Technologies previously expressed their intent to build an RTX mod; with that 2023 blog post also mentioning a co-op mode, which is now being added, an RTX addition might still be on the cards. Either way, the Community Edition's release is currently set for 2026, which doesn't give it a lot of time for final, ray-traced accoutrements, but we'll see.

#4097. Here are our PS Plus monthly games for November 2026

Dead Island 2! Tomb Raider! Monster Train 2!

Sony has announced the monthly games coming to PlayStation Plus Premium and Extra next month, bringing a mix of triple-A bangers and remastered classics to the service on the 3rd November. All are, of course, coming at the start of what is almost certainly going to be the biggest month of the year releases-wise.

Perhaps the biggest game on offer is Dead Island 2, Dambuster Studios and Deep Silver's first person zombie action game. There's plenty of grisly goodness here, and ample loot to snatch up and use against the undead hordes. It's a decent enough game, which should offer plenty of entertainment to those looking for something chunky to dig their teeth into while the Halloween spirit still lingers.

The remastered Tomb Raider Darkness Trilogy is not one to be skipped, especially if you're looking for a sizable time sink from your PlayStation Plus monthly games. While not known as being exactly the best Lara Croft games out there, Aspyr did some fine work polishing them up for modern platforms.

Finally we've got Monster Train 2. A deckbuilder roguelike that has you operating and managing trains where the forces of heaven and hell reside, all to defeat titans that threaten the orderly state of things. As the sole indie release on this monthly selection of PlayStation Plus games, it may be worth a try for those who can't get enough from the Roguelike genre even now. It even features a smug looking mushroom fella, how can you go wrong with that.

The reveal of these games coming to PlayStation Plus means the clock is ticking to grab October's offerings, many of which would fit well on the console of those getting into the spooky season.

For more information on PlayStation Plus, you can check out our guide to PS Plus and all the available games here.

#4096. Nintendo Is Currently Not Considering More Switch 2 Price Changes

Nintendo president, Shuntaro Furukawa, has confirmed that the company is currently not considering any further price changes for the Switch 2 following an increase earlier this year.

This comes via Reuters after Nintendo released its latest financial data, during which it was reported that sales for the Switch 2 dropped over 37% year-on-year, with operating profit sliding 16%.

Despite some concern amongst investors, Furukawa-san has sought to ease this by confirming that Nintendo is currently in a position to secure sufficient quantities of memory as the supply crisis continues.

Nintendo's forecast for the remainder of the fiscal year remains unchanged, so it's currently expecting to shift over 16 million Switch 2 units; a decline from last year, sure, but still an incredibly impressive figure.

Confirmation that no further price changes are on the horizon will no doubt come as a relief for many. The Switch 2's price rose globally earlier this year as a result of market conditions, which has no doubt contributed to the downward turn in sales.

You could certainly argue, however, that the price hike was relatively tame compared to some of the changes taking place at other companies. The Switch 2's price rose by $50 in the US and a mere £24 in the UK. Any price hike is disappointing, of course, but when you consider how expensive the PS5 and Xbox Series X|S are these days, it could be a lot worse.

#4095. Virtue and a Sledgehammer review – a haunting sci-fi drama about breaking walls, AI faces, and your heart

Outwardly about hitting things for stress relief, Virtue and a Sledgehammer is really an affecting family drama that confronts pain but doesn't give in to despair.

It’s been well over a week since my final swing of Virtue and a Sledgehammer’s righteous whacking stick, and I’m still finding it difficult to shift the game from my thoughtspace. Having tempted me in with promises of cathartic, base-instinct vengeance against a town of roboticised arseholes, it’s since had me picking through the rubble of my own demolition spree, not so much looking for meaning as trying to parse the abundance of it. I’d gladly invite you to join me in the wreckage.

Virtue’s developers, Selkie Harbour and the apparent nominative determinists at Deconstructeam – previously of The Cosmic Wheel Sisterhood – say it’s a "narrative exploration" game. Which is accurate, on both counts. As pictured sledgewielder Pratelle, your most urgent interactions involve breaking shit, be it the walls of your childhood hometown or the android copies of its former inhabitants. Really though, you’re bashing with purpose beyond your (or Pratelle’s) own satisfaction: hammering away masonry will open up new nooks and paths to explore, which in turn leads to more flashback story scenes, better contextualising a rampage that might otherwise seem lacking in justification.

This is not a swift process. Pratelle’s swings are slow and deliberate, each one needing at least some charging-up, and end on a similarly lengthy recovery animation. While this imbues encounters against the more aggressive bots with some timing-based challenge, the game’s sluggishness also serves to lend some emotional weight – a means of holding your head towards the crumbling homes and the clattering humanoids. Nothing dies here unless you absolutely, intentionally will it, and once you commit, there’s scant chance to do anything but watch as it hits the dirt.

On an initial playthrough, the techniques of fellow low-polyist Mouthwashing may come to mind: that game conveyed the cruelties of its main playable character through similarly slow, purposeful interactions. As Virtue gives up more of its secrets, though, it becomes clear that while it wants you to feel Pratelle’s rage, it also considers her crashout entirely legitimate. To explain fully would mean practising in spoilers, but those narrative shards seriously are worth tracking down, each scene laying on depth and tragic complexity to Pratelle and her family – the latter being the reason she’s back in town to begin with.

Non-chronological, but coherently written and arranged flashbacks run an impressively wide gamut of wholesomeness, unease, and horror. And they wisely take place before the sci-fi element becomes prevalent in the present-day storyline, keeping the darker moments more compellingly, uncomfortably grounded. Even with a tendency towards quip-speak, especially from the mouth of Nina, Pratelle’s smug genius of a sister, the mixing of fond memories with traumatic ones heightens the impact of both. It’s naturally awful to watch Nina coldly kick Pratelle out of their mother’s hospital room, or to see that mother inflict physical abuse on the sisters, but the hurt hits different when a later scene shows all three warmly chatting at home. Based on the chatter of their robot avatars, many of the family’s neighbours are/were variously racist, homophobic, or outright murderous, but it’s the pain and betrayal seeded in those past moments that drive Pratelle’s stomping, bludgeoning campaign of violence.

Crucially, Virtue does not introduce these humanising moments to manipulate you into manufactured, Far Cry 3-ass, you-are-the-real-monster guilt, and in-story attempts to play this trick on Pratelle herself are quickly called out as such. The wrongheaded people are wrong, the game knows it, and there’s no ulterior motive beyond the suggestion that those we love (and are loved by) can be corrupted by ego, ambition, or inherited trauma. Still, that central, lamentable family dynamic, and how skillfully its members are built up and broken apart in such short vignettes, are largely why I’m still pondering the game so much. I also confess to having replayed the entire thing, in far less brutal fashion, in the hope – proved vain – that it might help change some of their fates.

For better or worse, fury is the only language this town understands, and Pratelle is a fluent speaker. The long windup of attacks is at least met by an equal and opposite reaction of object-mangling: walls blast open with an appreciably exaggerated shower of debris, and taking out a building’s corners will cause a thunderous collapse of the entire structure. Thwacking robots isn’t quite as satisfying, in part because of the underwhelmingy dull 'thunk' of the impact sound, but a solid hit will still send them tumbling backwards with a deserved lack of grace. In some delightfully fortuitous melees, a clobbered bot would ragdoll hard enough into an adjacent wall to crack it open, revealing a memory shared I could have otherwise missed.

I briefly wondered if having me collect all these was necessary, given the game has no problem auto-triggering regular cutscenes at points. Except, it kind of is. Pratelle’s journey is cathartic, but it’s also a labour, the weight and sorrow of what she must do mirrored in her leaden footsteps and determined but joyless sledgehammering. It’s entirely appropriate, then, that uncovering her full story takes some extra effort, just as that effort is entirely rewarded.

Virtue and a Sledgehammer stands against much. It’s anti-prejudice, anti-ambivalence, and in not very subtle terms, anti-AI: its depiction of a soulless (albeit human-driven) machine takeover, complete with whining about how hard life was before, throws up gladly smashable parallels to the chatbot infestation of creative and public spaces.

For all its violent opposition, though, it’s also earnestly, maybe even optimistically pro-human. While drawing a line at intentional and misguided evils, it’s accepting of our imperfections and the role they have in shaping us – remember you’re fighting about 600 identical automatons – and only plumbs the depths of true despair when humanity isn’t adequately defended. Rage is vented and steam is let off, but not in a purely spiteful, fuck-the-world manner, and even Pratelle is only tearing her past down so she can move on from it. Maybe one day I will too, if I can ever get her stupid, fascinating game out of my head.

#4094. "This company has been driven into a wall for years" - Life is Strange studio Don't Nod faces unrest while teetering on insolvency

"For two years, employees have been living on the edge."

There's deep unrest at French studio Don't Nod - creator of Life is Strange, Remember Me, Vampyr, Banishers: New Eden, and most recently Aphelion - as it scrambles to restructure itself and guard against insolvency.

Indeed, an impassioned account of proceedings on French union Le Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Vidéo's website (via Rock, Paper, Shotgun) reveals Don't Nod has entered safeguard proceedings - a kind of last-ditch restructuring effort to stave off insolvency. It also reports that even though redundancies are being made,Don't Nod intends to finish making the in-development game codenamed P14, albeit relying more on outsourced development rather than its cut-down in-house team.

The report, which claims knowledge of a memo sent by Don't Nod CEO Oskar Guilbert, and of the goings-on of the Don't Nod employee representatives - the CSE - doubts whether Don't Nod will be able to finish the game. Apparently all of the studio's character artists, concept artists, most of its environment artists, most of its sound designers, game designers, level designers, programmers, producers, testers, and dev-ops have been let go.

"To compensate for this massacre and keep on running with production on a game that, to this day, didn't cut down on its scope and is keeping around a hundred persons busy, management is betting it all on outsourcing," the report says.

"Managers, who are usually seen as more competent and experienced than non-managers, are kept within the organisation and studio management expects them to orchestrate the massive shift to outsourcing as well as take over the workload of the fired team members. Anyone with a little experience with video games production and sanity understands how out-of-touch such a plan is."

The report also claims Don't Nod management isn't able to offer affected staff severance packages or redundancy plans. "It'll be the strict legal minimum and you'll be glad for it," the report said. A voluntary redundancy scheme also isn't reportedly being offered.

"This company has been driven into a wall for years, against all outsider wisdom, against any sort of reality-based assessment," the report went on. "For two years, employees have been living on the edge, in uncertainty and anxiety, all of it reinforced by internal comms that alternated between inexistence and outright lies. This impacted their health, as evidenced by the CSE who documented six workplace accidents in 2026 and recently had to launch an inquiry into a serious and imminent danger.

"They do not care about the damage it deals to employees' health, they made no risk prevention plan. Employees feel like hostages to a radicalised management, who keep playing with the livelihood and the future of 140 people with no care for the consequences of their actions."

The CSE negotiations apparently end on 3rd November. We've asked Don't Nod for a comment.

News of Don't Nod's slide towards the brink of insolvency comes a month after the company's board voted to enter a period of restructuring - of transformation - that could lead to lay-offs for as many as 90 people. That in turn came only a few months after Don't Nod said it was close to running out of money.

The company's most recent game, Aphelion (released in April) - which charted a duo's escape across a sci-fi world - struggled to find an audience. We didn't review it on Eurogamer but a brief look around shows it only received middling scores. 2025's Life is Strange follow-up Lost Records fared better - we awarded it four out of five stars - but its success wasn't enough to properly propel the studio.

#4093. Street Fighter V temporarily delisted and online functions turned off due to issues caused by last week's PHP security flaw

Though Street Fighter 6 has been the most popular fighting game in the world for three years running, there are still dedicated soldiers playing Street Fighter V right now. Be that due to its much larger character roster (thanks to many more years of updates, obviously, but I do personally miss G), its unique V-Skill and V-Trigger mechanics, or people just not liking Drive Rush or throw loops in 6, the playerbase is still very much there. Unfortunately, that playerbase is currently facing the consequences of the PHP programming language vulnerability and subsequent security-led shutdowns across online services from the last week onwards, as Street Fighter V's online functionality has been shut down until it can be ensured to be secure. It's also been temporarily delisted, effectively taking it off sale, from Steam.

In a statement posted to Twitter, developer-publishers Capcom stated that "Emergency maintenance is currently underway to address this issue. Until the fix has been completed, sales on the PlayStation Store and Steam will be suspended in stages." Capcom weren't specific in exactly how the game could be vulnerable, but considering the (seemingly unrelated) data breach the Capcom ID service suffered last week, perhaps they wish to stay tight-lipped on security vulnerabilities for the time being.

Street Fighter V remains accessible for those who already own it, minus the online functionality. No endless grinding away in ranked or buying costumes for now, which is probably for the best. There's still Arcade Mode! It took them three years to add it, but it's there now!

All this did also let me see a truly hilarious Twitter reply, which I do want to share: "You lying corpo cunts ain't gonna fix shit, you're trying to force us to play 6!" God, why didn't Capcom think of that before? Street Fighter 6 has totally, definitely been struggling for players, so the most appropriate response is to shut down Street Fighter V and use an internet-spanning security flaw as an excuse. A devious plan, indeed.

#4092. "This is a serious incident": Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 devs Warhorse hit by cyberattack targeting their systems and data

Studio working to lock things down and work out how breach happened

Kingdom Come Deliverance 2 developers Warhorse, who're also working on a Lord of the Rings RPG, have revealed that they've been targeted by a cyberattack aiming to access their systems and data. The studio are currently working to make sure their locks are all clicked back into place and tolearn exactly how the incident happened.

"Warhorse Studios confirms that it has been the target of a cyberattack," the studio announced a statement posted to their website. "We are working with cybersecurity experts to secure our systems, investigate the incident, and assess its full impact. The attack involved unauthorized access to company systems as well as access to company data. We are coordinating with the relevant authorities as the investigation continues."

"This is a serious incident for Warhorse Studios and everyone affected," CEO Martin Frývaldský added. "Our immediate priority is to secure our systems, establish the full extent of the breach, and take the necessary steps to protect our employees, partners, and community. We are dedicating the resources needed to address this situation and will communicate further information as soon as we responsibly can."

The studio don't plan on offering any further comments until they've got more "verified information" to share, so one would assume we'll next be hearing from them once their investigation's run its course or drawn some concrete conclusions beyond what was outlined in these statements.

That's not too surprising, given Warhorse seem to have potentially gone public about this attack at an earlier stage than, for example, Capcom did with the Capcom ID data breach they suffered the other week. Obviously, no company wants unwanted intruders getting ahold of any of their stuff regardless of what it is, but in the games industry there's the risk of bits of games being leaked prematurely on top of all of the other problems a successful attack could lead to. CD Projekt Red, Insomniac, and Rockstar are among the studios a quick glance back through the archives have turned up as sufferers of cyberattacks or hacks in the not too distant past. In each case, the attack precipitated serious headaches for not just the companies, but the staff working hard to make their games.

It's unclear if this Warhorse cyberattack is any way linked to a recent uptick in AI-enabled hacking, as the world continues to become a less nice place to live by the minute thanks to the tech.

Here's hoping the studio are able to make sure things are secure again quickly and that their workers haven't been affected too badly by this attack.

#4091. Demanding 300GB to install despite its actual size of 145GB, Phantom Blade Zero makes me question what a gigabyte is worth

We're not in a very cheap era for PC parts. A (possibly manufactured!) GPU shortage making cards that can actually run modern games near-inaccessible to the vast majority of people, combined with RAM and SSDs just generally being horrifically expensive due to demand for their use in data centers, is making contemporary games with high performance requirements very difficult for some people to justify even trying to run, let alone buy. S-Game's recent reveal of wuxia action game Phantom Blade Zero's preload guide and system requirements has brought this to mind, alongside bringing tears to my eyes, as the game requires not only an SSD to run at all, and 145GB to install, but 300GB of free space to pre-load.

Genuinely, what are we doing here. The guide states that this is because "temporary files and the complete game must coexist during the unlock process", and that "once the process is complete, storage usage will drop to approximately 145GB." Oh, sure, just a small install then. 145GB is already a ridiculous size for one game — I know that commenters will tell me that this has become somewhat standard, but that is not reasonable or a good thing — and requiring players to free up double the actual install size just to get the damn thing on your system remains absurd. Deputy ed/former hardware ed James says this is probably a quirk of how Unreal Engine 5, specifically, handles updates. I asked him if there was anything else wrong with UE5 and he began staring into space.

Anyway, there's a lot of things that happen in games that makes me say something along the lines of 'fuck'. Constant layoffs, AI's tendrils being spread everywhere, CEOs telling me and their staff that it'll save their company. But this is something different, in which I stare at my monitor, read those system requirements again and just want to scream 'what the FUCK?' Phantom Blade Zero could be the greatest game ever made (it seems to be pretty good, if the recent reviews are anything to go by), but no game could ever be worth 300GB. Again, what are we doing. That's like, uh, sixty Devil May Cry 3s.

#4090. AMD FSR Upscaling 4.1 Has Officially Arrived For Xbox Series X|S

"We can't wait to see what developers create with it."

A couple of weeks ago, the folks at AMD made headlines when they announced that AMD FSR 4.1 would be coming to Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S in the near future, and the rollout has officially begun today!

As a result of this, developers will have access to a new method of improving visual fidelity (and in some cases boosting performance) in their games across both consoles, which should prove particularly useful when it comes to the lower-powered Xbox Series S.

"Working closely with AMD, the XBOX team has optimized AMD FSR™ Upscaling 4 for XBOX Series X|S, making ML-based upscaling practical on the consoles' RDNA 2-based GPUs. These optimizations enable developers to benefit from improved image quality while balancing GPU performance, helping them deliver better visual experiences on existing XBOX hardware."

"The new Microsoft GDK sample demonstrates how to integrate FSR4 across XBOX Series X|S and Windows using AMD’s FSR SDK. It includes both Full and Lite INT8 models, allowing developers to explore different rendering resolutions and evaluate the tradeoffs between image quality and performance."

Of course, it's still early days right now and we don't have any real-world examples of AMD FSR 4.1 working on XBOX Series X|S just yet, but we assume developers of all kinds will start integrating it into their games going forward.

Not only should this lead to improved experiences in demanding XBOX Series X|S titles, but it should also mean the two consoles remain capable for many years to come, even after Project Helix arrives in the next generation.

As for your comparison with QSSR, it is currently only supported by two games on PS5: Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei. At this stage, it is mostly a marketing feature with very little real impact for players. In reality, AMD's QSSR is derived from FSR, but in a much more limited form because, as you mentioned, the base PS5 lacks some native hardware features that are available on the Xbox Series consoles.

Furthermore, it is more complex for third-party developers, as it requires genuine porting work. As a result, this technology will likely remain limited to a small number of PlayStation-exclusive titles.

FSR, on the other hand, is a technology that has been deployed much more broadly by game developers, as it is already widely used on PC.

The case of PlayStation's PSSR, which is only available on the PS5 Pro, is different. The PS5 Pro already includes more native hardware capabilities than the base PS5 and is significantly more powerful. Even then, PSSR is also derived from FSR 4, although it still does not match FSR 4 at equivalent hardware performance levels. PSSR has seen greater adoption among developers, but the numbers remain relatively modest in practice. We're talking about roughly 200 games that support PSSR, which is still a small figure compared to the total number of games released each year.

What is certain is that PlayStation's marketing around GTA VI is misleading, or at the very least requires significant nuance. If we're talking about the base PS5, then the claim is false: GTA VI would run better on Xbox Series consoles with FSR 4.1.2. On PS5 Pro, however, GTA VI would likely perform better, which is hardly surprising given that it is a more powerful mid-generation refresh released later and sold at a significantly higher price. However, its price-to-performance ratio remains relatively poor.

Given the relatively small install base of the PS5 Pro compared to the standard PS5, the Xbox Series remains the most obvious value-for-money choice for the majority of players interested in GTA VI.

The claim that GTA VI or other games runs better on PS5 is simply false, on the contrary.

#4089. Sony Has Secured Enough Memory to Meet Console Demand Through March 2028

Amid ever-increasing hardware prices, driven by an AI-led drain on memory components, Sony has reassured investors that it’s secured enough inventory to meet its hardware projections through March 2028.

In its new financial report, the manufacturer acknowledged the following:

“Regarding memory procurement for next fiscal year, based on discussions held so far with various suppliers, we have aligned on the quantity of memory needed for our projected hardware unit sales.”

Obviously we don’t know what its projections for the next fiscal year are just yet, and whether it’ll need to adjust the price of the PS5 again in the new year. But it will at least have inventory to ship, which is important.

It’s going to be really interesting to see whether its next fiscal year will include the PS6 or not.

Sony says it’s making “solid progress” on the system, but it’s still unclear whether it’ll ship in 2027 or later.

Xbox, for the record, has said it plans to ship a new handheld in 2027 and its next console in 2028. Its price could run as high as $1,800 – although it’s expected the PS6 will be cheaper to manufacture overall. (Although potentially still $1,000+.)

This is a tricky period for manufacturers of all consumer electronics, but PS5’s enormous captive install base has shielded it slightly from the repercussions so far.

In its latest fiscal report, it revealed an 83% increase to its operating income, meaning the profitability of PlayStation is in an extremely steady and healthy position right now.

#4088. Cyberpunk 2 might include multiplayer after CD Projekt Red scrapped the feature in Cyberpunk 2077

Cyberpunk 2 might try to revive Cyberpunk 2077's online ambitions, as a new CD Projekt Red job listing is looking for someone familiar with "multiplayer network architecture."

As spotted by Cheap Happens, the role-playing powerhouse is currently looking to hire a lead quest programmer for its upcoming open-world sequel. Buried away at the bottom of the job listing, under the "Nice To Haves" section, the studio asks for an "understanding of multiplayer network architecture and client-server synchronization for game state/ quests."

The multiplayer mention is by no means confirmation that Cyberpunk 2 - or whatever it ends up being called - will have co-op and other online modes, but it's definitely something CD Projekt Red is looking into. And it certainly makes sense, too.

Once upon a time, Cyberpunk 2077 was intended to receive a multiplayer portion sometime after its initial launch. Of course, at the time, the shaky state of the game's development meant that was no longer feasible and CD Projekt Red instead said multiplayer would come as its own "triple-A release." Eventually, the famed studio realised it simply had to focus on ensuring the base game was stable enough on its own, and shelved those online ambitions.

A few years back, Cyberpunk 2077's senior quest designer, Philipp Weber, told Eurogamer the company was "focusing on bringing online into all of our franchises one day" by "building an online technology that can be seamlessly integrated into development of our future games."

More recently, in 2024, CD Projekt CEO Adam Badowski said the team were "considering" multiplayer elements for the Cyberpunk sequel back when the game was still in its early concept phases.

We don't know much else about the neon-drenched follow-up, but CDPR has been keeping series fans full and fed with continual updates to Cyberpunk 2077. Earlier this week, the game got an update celebrating the debut of Cyberpunk Edgerunners Season 2 on Netflix - everything from dual-wielding to cross-platform mods were added to the six-year-old game.

#4087. Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced is wrapping things up with one last big update that adds in new game plus and a throwback to the original game

Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced is setting sail for quieter pastures. That's because the game's last big update arrived today, with Ubisoft explaining that there are only plans for quality-of-life updates for the game going forward. Still, it's a meaty enough sounding update, and one that could in theory keep you going forever if you'd like to torture yourself by relegating your life to a single video game.

Well, maybe not forever. This update is introducing new game plus, letting you replay the game from the start, if you're the kind of person that somehow has time for that. It'll be possible to do this up to five times, with each subsequent playthrough increasing the difficulty level. You'll get to hang on to things like tools, weapons, upgrades for the Jackdaw, outfits, hideout progression, codex items and more besides.

With new game plus also comes a new difficulty setting, nightmare mode, which "transforms Black Flag Resynced into a brutal fight for survival where every duel can be your last. Enemies react faster, hit harder, and punish hesitation. The Caribbean is as beautiful as ever, but beneath the waves and beyond the horizon, death awaits the unprepared." Parrying timing is also reduced in this mode, there's no more white glint on enemy attacks, and the one-shot kill safety is disabled. On the stealth front, deduction time is greatly reduced and enemies can hear you when you're moving faster than anything above a walk.

Beyond this, a number of community chests have been hidden around the game, "some with special community requested rewards." You can also expect some new, or technically old, takedowns; "We have brought back takedown animations from the original game, including hidden blade, unarmed, single sword and gunblade takedowns." There's also some new cosmetics, and a good range of bug fixes. You can read about all of that over on Ubisoft's website.

This all comes the same month that Ubisoft laid off 70 workers at Ubisoft Singapore, the lead developer on Black Flag Resynced. Solidarity with all those affected.

#4085. A leaked trailer for Transformers: Reactivate shows off the only lick of gameplay we'll likely ever see of the cancelled co-op action game

Back in 2022, Gears Tactics studio Splash Damage revealed that they were working on a Transformers game. It was called Transformers: Reactivate, and at the time was set to be a 1-4 player co-op action game, but come 2025 and the game gets canned all while parent company Tencent was going on a funding withdrawal spree in the games industry. Nothing substantial was ever really shown off of the game, but a trailer has now been leaked featuring what was apparently meant to be an internal look at it in action.

The trailer was shared by a Gwitter user called Nem who is devoted to "archiving and preserving Transformers: Reactivate because I need to cope somehow." Prior to the trailer itself, a message from Nem explained: "The following is an internal trailer not meant for the public, the music in it was released on October 21st 2024, placing this trailer at most three months prior to cancellation. With Tencent having pulled out in June/July 2024, this leads us to believe this trailer was made as part of an investment pitch to other publishers that ultimately failed."

Full credit for this discovery goes to @EnderGuyZV2!! TRANSFORMERS REACTIVATE GAMEPLAY TRAILER!!From around October-November 2024! This is our first glimpse at what the $70 game was hoping for, and hopefully we learn more about this version as time goes on. pic.twitter.com/52GhgTUrtz

Apparently by the time this trailer had been made, the game had shifted gears into a premium release, moving away from being a free-to-play live service game, complete with a story campaign that could be played solo or in online co-op. And the result is certainly a fairly real looking 2020s video game, at the very least. It's got some shooting, it's got some driving, it's got some shooting while driving, though it has surprisingly little actual transforming. Perhaps they were still ironing out the kinks mechanically and animationally.

This is one of those weird things where a big licensed game feels like it should have been a slam dunk, if only it had come out 10 years prior and wasn't catered towards the curse that is live service in the first place. I'm also always oddly eeked out by leaked trailers, not from some weird moral perspective, but because it's evidence of something existing, and yet is entirely impossible to engage with. What other medium has anything like this? Weird! I look forward to someone figuring out the solution to this. I'd suggest starting with dismantling capitalism, perhaps.

#4084. Alien: Isolation 2 devs commit to a physical edition: "Staying true to the analogue nature of Alien is one of our pillars"

And the Xenomorph's "even more intelligent" this time.

The developers behind Alien: Isolation 2 are committing to a full physical edition, and have shared even more details about the highly-anticipated survival horror sequel.

In a recent developer Q&A posted today (below), developers from Creative Assembly shed even more light on their shadowy follow-up to 2014's fan-favorite horror game. When asked if the sequel would get a physical edition, the devs simply said "yes" and explained that "staying true to the analogue nature of Alien is one of our pillars."

Throughout the video, the Creative Assembly team reiterated that so much of their inspiration comes from Ridley Scott's seminal sci-fi classic from 1979, naturally, which influenced their decision to release a physical boxed version of the game and to keep the focus on one ever present, highly intelligent and always frightening Xenomorph.

Confirmation of a physical release comes months after Sony announced plans to end production of new PlayStation discs in 2028 - a decision that led to heated backlash from players, physical distributors and consumer rights groups.

The only wrinkle is that Alien: Isolation 2 doesn't have a release date at the moment. Should it release any later than February, 2028, PlayStation players probably won't be able to get their hands on a proper disc - though the game is also launching across PC, Nintendo Switch 2 and Xbox Series X/S.

Elsewhere in the dev vlog, creative director Al Hope explained how the team is expanding on the original game's famously tight level design. "You have the interior spaces which feel claustrophobic and the player feels trapped, which is super familiar to Isolation fans. But we also have exteriors as well where the creature is now learning to adapt and hunt in these open spaces," Hope said.

"I really love the idea that the player will feel trapped and claustrophobic in the interiors and actually really want to get outside. Once they manage to do that, after that initial relief and sense of a small victory, they will start very slowly to feel really exposed and vulnerable and actually quite like to go back inside again. And really, playing on that roller coaster and see-saw of emotion and motivation - that's a big part of what Alien: Isolation 2 is."

James Green, lead game designer, also said roughly "a quarter to a third of the team worked on the original," while all new developers helped to bring a fresh perspective onboard. And, somehow, the Xenomorph is "even more intelligent" this time; scarily capable of using the extreme climate to hide and hunt you.

If you're in the mood to play something that'll get those heart rates way up this month, check out our picks of the spookiest Halloween games.

#4082. UK-based Rockstar devs will be putting their union recognition to a vote during GTA 6's launch next month

The vote will also be held when closing arguments will be made for the ongoing employment tribunal

November is potentially going to be big for Rockstar Games, and not just because of that GTA 6 thing they're doing. As shared in a press release from the Independent Workers of Great Britain (IWGB), recognition of the IWGB Union at Rockstar will be voted upon by staffers at the studio, with votes being held from November 12th (a week before GTA 6's launch date) and November 26th.

"The terms of the recognition deal, agreed upon by workers and management, would give workers a say over topics including pay and bonuses, overtime, redundancies, flexible working arrangements, and generative AI policies," the press release explains. It also notes that if the vote is successful, the union will become the largest recognised union in the UK games industry.

This also comes at another pivotal time for Rockstar workers, both current and former alike. Almost exactly a year ago, Rockstar laid off 31 staffers in an alleged act of union busting. Fast forward to now, and an employment tribunal is being held between the game developer, the IWGB, and the laid off workers. Closing arguments for the tribunal will take place between November 17th and 18th, mere days ahead of the game's launch. It'll still be a while until a judge decides if Rockstar did break employment law.

In a statement, Rockstar Game Workers Union Committee Member Shanti Easton-Steel said, "For me, this vote comes down to ensuring employees at Rockstar get honesty and openness surrounding the decisions that affect them. When management choices are kept hidden, we can’t properly address issues like the gender pay gap, the uneven and ever-changing policies on overtime pay, or the concerns many co-workers hold around job security post-release."

Solidarity with the workers as always. GTA 6 will undoubtedly be the biggest game of the decade, and everyone that has worked on it deserves to be properly compensated and assuaged of their concerns.

#4081. Discord know they replaced forums, so they're making your messages in discoverable servers searchable, which immediately raises one question: what about AI?

The changes start coming into effect next month

You might want to hold off on that horny posting in your favourite discoverable Discord server. The chat service announced today that any servers that are listed as discoverable, meaning anyone can find them simply through Googling, no invite link required, will now also show messages and discussions posted in said servers on Google.

This is being done because, as Discord admits, forums aren't as popular these days. "Prior to Discord's launch, message boards were common, ranging from community-driven forums to official ones run by game studios," reads a post explaining the update. "These message boards excelled at hosting long-form, structured conversations about helping people, theory crafting, and more. While they still exist today, many have moved into Discord servers. This has led to valuable information being locked in Discord conversations, inaccessible to the wider internet. We want to fix this."

I have certainly seen this complaint myself on a number of occasions, so, to a certain degree I'm sure this will be welcome. It does immediately raise one concern for me though, that being everyone's favourite topic at the moment: AI. As it currently stands, it's Discord policy that AI companies are not allowed to train their models on a user's messages. How does this change with these messages now being publicly available? What safeguards will be put in place to prevent this, if any?

As the post explains, discoverable servers will have server web pages where messages and discussions can be found through your search engine of choice. Every discoverable server will have a server web page from November 16th, next month, but you can opt out ahead of time and once the feature is live. It's from mid-December where channel messages will be viewable on these server web pages. "Server admins decide which channels take part, and server members can choose whether their own messages appear. Usernames and avatars will not be shown alongside these messages," the post notes.

Also worth noting is that in "the EU, UK, Canada, Brazil, Australia, and South Korea, the member setting for Channel Messages is off by default given legal restrictions, so members’ messages won’t appear on the web unless they turn it on. Users in the teen age group are excluded completely and cannot enable Channel Messages until they’re an adult. Everywhere else, it’s on unless members turn it off."

On the one hand, sure, it'll be nice to have some of this information that was previously much harder to access publicly available. On the other, the open web is infested with corporations that are looking to harvest your data without any consequences, currently, and now something as simple as sending a Discord message could potentially aid in that. I'm glad that you have individual control over whether your own messages get seen, I just struggle to see this as an overwhelmingly positive move.

#4080. 'Aggressive Investment in Entertainment Is Paying Off': Sony Lifts Profit Outlook After Strong Quarter

Sony’s transition away from electronics and into entertainment is paying serious dividends, after a killer quarter has prompted it to lift its operating income outlook for the fiscal year through March 2027.

The Japanese giant now expects to pull ¥1.87 trillion (~$11.8 billion) in profit, up 15% on its previous prediction.

In its Q2 report, the period spanning July 206 through September 2026, it posted operating income of ¥622.3 billion (~$3.9 billion) alone, beating pretty much all analyst predictions.

At the time of writing, its stock price is up 7% on the back of these results.

Hideki Yasuda of Toyo Research and Advice Co told Bloomberg:

"Today’s results clearly show the payoff from Sony’s aggressive investment in content over the past several years, across movies, games and music. When Sony was more hardware-driven, its earnings were much more volatile."

As mentioned, Sony can thank its investment into entertainment for the positive results, at a time when the consumer electronics market is strained due to component prices.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day, the acclaimed Tom Holland movie, was a huge win for Sony Pictures, meanwhile PlayStation continued its momentum with another excellent quarter for PS5.

Sony Music also saw increases on the back of its co-ownership of Michael Jackson’s music catalogue, which saw an enormous increase in streams due to the release of the Michael biopic earlier in the year.

Despite all these wins in entertainment, the firm’s image sensing business also saw improvements to profitability, despite a global decline in smartphone sales.

All things said, the Japanese company finds itself in an incredibly healthy position, and its big business bets all appear to be paying off at the moment.
